entry.title: [law] Supreme Court blocks Fifth Circuit order, preserves mifepristone access by mail while Louisiana lawsuit proceeds through lower courts
entry.summary: The Supreme Court on May 14 granted a stay of the Fifth Circuit's order that would have reinstated in-person dispensing requirements for mifepristone, preserving nationwide mail-order and telehealth access to the abortion pill while Louisiana's lawsuit against the FDA continues in the lower courts, with Justices Thomas and Alito dissenting.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The Supreme Court on May 14 granted a stay of the Fifth Circuit's order that would have reinstated in-person dispensing requirements for mifepristone, preserving nationwide mail-order and telehealth access to the abortion pill while Louisiana's lawsuit against the FDA continues in the lower courts, with Justices Thomas and Alito dissenting.

Louisiana filed suit last fall asking federal courts to reinstate the in-person dispensing requirement that the FDA relaxed in 2021, allowing mifepristone to be prescribed via telehealth and sent by mail or dispensed at retail pharmacies. A three-judge Fifth Circuit panel sided with Louisiana on May 1, 2026, temporarily reinstating the in-person requirement. Justice Samuel Alito, who handles emergency applications from the Fifth Circuit, issued a series of administrative stays pausing that order — first through May 11, then extended through May 14 — while Danco Laboratories and GenBioPro's emergency applications were before the full Court. On May 14, the full Court granted the stay, with only Justices Thomas and Alito dissenting publicly; Alito wrote separately calling the majority order "unreasoned" and "remarkable." The case now returns to the Fifth Circuit for expedited proceedings on the merits of Louisiana's claim that its sovereignty interest entitles it to impose prescribing requirements on an FDA-approved drug beyond what federal law mandates.

Why it matters: This is the second major Supreme Court proceeding over mifepristone in two years: the 2024 ruling in FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine dismissed the prior challenge on standing grounds, but the Court's reasoning explicitly left open the possibility that states with direct regulatory interests could bring their own suits, which Louisiana then did. The current case presents a major preemption question about whether states can impose prescribing restrictions on FDA-approved medications beyond what federal law requires — a question with implications well beyond abortion medication for any federally approved drug that states might seek to restrict independently. The Trump administration's ongoing internal safety review of mifepristone adds a parallel track: if FDA reinstates restrictions administratively, it could moot the litigation, but any such action would face its own legal challenge. If the Fifth Circuit rules for Louisiana on the merits, the Supreme Court will take the case with full briefing and likely resolve the federal-state preemption question before the 2026 elections — a politically significant timeline given the issue's electoral salience in states with tight Senate and House races.

entry.title: [law] Republican legislators urge Supreme Court not to intervene in Virginia redistricting fight, arguing Democrats forfeited federal claims by never raising them in state proceedings
entry.summary: Republican members of Virginia's legislature filed a May 14 brief urging the Supreme Court not to stay the Virginia Supreme Court's ruling that invalidated a mid-cycle redistricting amendment on procedural grounds, arguing that Democrats waived any federal constitutional claims by failing to raise them during the state court proceedings.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Republican members of Virginia's legislature filed a May 14 brief urging the Supreme Court not to stay the Virginia Supreme Court's ruling that invalidated a mid-cycle redistricting amendment on procedural grounds, arguing that Democrats waived any federal constitutional claims by failing to raise them during the state court proceedings.

In April 2026, Virginia voters approved by roughly 3 percentage points a constitutional amendment allowing the General Assembly to redraw congressional maps outside the decennial cycle. The Virginia Supreme Court invalidated the referendum on May 8, finding that the General Assembly violated state constitutional procedures: amendments must pass in two separate legislative sessions separated by a House of Delegates election, but the General Assembly voted on the amendment after voters had already begun casting early ballots in the 2025 election, meaning the statutory sequencing requirement was not met. Governor Abigail Spanberger announced Virginia would not use the new map in 2026 elections. Attorney General Jay Jones filed an emergency application with the US Supreme Court to stay the Virginia ruling and allow the more Democratic-favorable map to take effect for the 2026 midterms. Republican legislators filed a response on May 14 arguing that federal courts should not intervene because the challengers failed to preserve any federal constitutional claims in the state proceedings, and separately that state courts applying state constitutional amendment-ratification procedures do not present a reviewable federal question.

Why it matters: The procedural forfeiture argument is potentially dispositive: if the Supreme Court agrees that Democrats did not preserve federal claims below, it can deny the stay without reaching the merits of whether the Virginia Supreme Court correctly applied its own constitutional procedures — a much faster and narrower resolution. The timing is acute because Virginia election officials need a final congressional map by mid-May to begin ballot preparation for June primaries and the November general elections, so a delay in Supreme Court action effectively defaults to the prior (more Republican-favorable) map. The underlying substantive question — whether a state court's application of its own amendment-ratification rules can ever present a federal constitutional question — sits at an unusual intersection of federalism doctrine and elections law that the Supreme Court has not directly addressed. The case is part of a broader pattern of redistricting litigation becoming a permanent feature of the Court's emergency docket, with both parties using last-minute applications to lock in or block maps before elections, often without full briefing on the underlying constitutional questions.

entry.title: [law] Australia's High Court hears first-ever climate case: whether a coal mine's scope-3 overseas emissions count as local environmental impacts requiring assessment under NSW planning law
entry.summary: On May 13, Australia's High Court heard the country's first-ever climate change case, weighing whether the approval of the Mount Pleasant coal mine expansion was unlawful because it failed to assess the local climate impacts of the mine's scope-3 emissions — the greenhouse gases released when exported coal is burned overseas — which represent an estimated 98% of the project's total lifetime greenhouse output.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

On May 13, Australia's High Court heard the country's first-ever climate change case, weighing whether the approval of the Mount Pleasant coal mine expansion was unlawful because it failed to assess the local climate impacts of the mine's scope-3 emissions — the greenhouse gases released when exported coal is burned overseas — which represent an estimated 98% of the project's total lifetime greenhouse output.

The case is MACH Energy Australia v. Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group Inc (DAMS HEG), brought by a Hunter Valley grassroots community group challenging the 2023 NSW Independent Planning Commission approval of the Mount Pleasant open-cut coal mine expansion near Muswellbrook. At issue is whether NSW's Environmental Planning and Assessment Act required regulators to consider scope-3 emissions — the greenhouse gases released when exported coal is burned by overseas buyers — which for the Mount Pleasant project represent approximately 98% of total lifetime emissions. The community group argued these downstream emissions cause locally felt climate impacts through increased temperatures, altered precipitation, and heightened flood and bushfire risk in the Hunter Valley. The NSW Court of Appeal ruled unanimously in July 2025 that the mine's approval was unlawful and that planning authorities are legally required to consider specific local climate impacts of a project's downstream emissions. MACH Energy appealed, and the High Court heard arguments May 13 on whether scope-3 emissions constitute an environmental impact "in the locality" under the statutory language — the key phrase on which the entire legal analysis turns.

Why it matters: This is the most consequential climate litigation case in Australia's history and is being closely watched in comparable jurisdictions worldwide. If the High Court upholds the NSW Court of Appeal, it will establish that Australian planning law mandates full lifecycle emissions analysis for fossil fuel approvals, forcing reassessment of pending and recently approved coal and gas projects worth tens of billions of dollars and raising the evidentiary bar for any new fossil fuel development in Australia. A High Court reversal would signal that diffuse global climate effects cannot satisfy a "in the locality" statutory threshold, insulating a broad class of fossil fuel projects from climate-based legal challenges and potentially slowing analogous proceedings in the UK, Netherlands, Germany, and the United States — all of which are litigating whether planning and permitting law requires scope-3 emissions accounting. The ICJ's recent landmark advisory opinion establishing state obligations to prevent climate harm provides additional international legal context in which the High Court is deciding, and the justices are aware their ruling will set a binding national precedent on one of the most consequential environmental law questions in Australian jurisprudence.

entry.title: [cybersecurity] TanStack npm supply chain attack breaches OpenAI and Mistral codebases; threat actor TeamPCP steals signing certificates from two OpenAI employee Mac devices in two attack waves
entry.summary: A supply chain attack poisoned 84 npm package artifacts in TanStack — an open-source JavaScript ecosystem with over 12 million weekly downloads — compromising two OpenAI employee Mac devices and Mistral AI's codebase management system in two attack phases on April 29 and May 11, with threat actor TeamPCP exfiltrating signing certificates and credential material before OpenAI detected and contained the incident.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

A supply chain attack poisoned 84 npm package artifacts in TanStack — an open-source JavaScript ecosystem with over 12 million weekly downloads — compromising two OpenAI employee Mac devices and Mistral AI's codebase management system in two attack phases on April 29 and May 11, with threat actor TeamPCP exfiltrating signing certificates and credential material before OpenAI detected and contained the incident.

The threat actor TeamPCP injected malware into 84 TanStack npm artifacts in two waves, with the malware designed to steal credentials and self-propagate to other packages maintained by compromised developers. OpenAI confirmed that two employee Mac devices were breached, affecting limited source code repositories in its iOS, macOS, and Windows product lines; the company stated it "observed activity consistent with the malware's publicly described behavior, including unauthorized access and credential-focused exfiltration activity" but found no evidence of customer data theft. Mistral AI also confirmed its codebase management system was affected. The attacker targeted application signing certificates — the credentials macOS uses to verify that software comes from an identified developer and has not been tampered with. OpenAI responded by isolating affected systems, revoking all user sessions, rotating credentials, reviewing software notarizations, and asking macOS users who have not updated the ChatGPT app since April 2026 to do so by June 12 or lose support and updates. TeamPCP had previously attacked LiteLLM and the European Commission using stolen Amazon API credentials.

Why it matters: Supply chain attacks via package registries are among the most potent attack vectors in modern software because a single poisoned package reaches millions of downstream projects instantly without requiring the attacker to target each victim directly. The theft of application signing certificates is particularly consequential for macOS: Apple's Gatekeeper security framework relies on those certificates to verify that applications are authentic and unmodified, meaning stolen signing credentials allow attackers to distribute malicious applications that appear legitimate to users and security tools alike. The involvement of two leading frontier AI companies — OpenAI and Mistral — in the same attack by the same threat actor suggests TeamPCP may be specifically targeting AI companies' proprietary code, model training pipelines, or internal tooling, rather than treating them as incidental victims of a broad supply chain sweep. The June 12 update deadline leaves a defined population of potentially still-vulnerable macOS users exposed, and the fact that the attack persisted across two waves weeks apart raises questions about detection capability. TeamPCP's prior targeting of the European Commission adds a geopolitical dimension that US and EU regulators may invoke when pushing for stronger mandatory supply chain security standards under the EU's Cyber Resilience Act and the forthcoming US AI security framework.

entry.title: [tech law] OpenAI endorses Kids Online Safety Act — Techdirt argues the move is regulatory capture that prices out AI competitors, deflects AI-specific regulation, and manages reputational exposure from ChatGPT harm lawsuits
entry.summary: OpenAI's Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane publicly endorsed the Kids Online Safety Act this week, a move Techdirt analyzes as a three-part strategic maneuver: imposing compliance costs that price out smaller AI competitors, redirecting legislative attention from AI-specific bills to social media regulation, and generating political cover for reputational damage from lawsuits alleging ChatGPT companion products contributed to youth suicides.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

OpenAI's Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane publicly endorsed the Kids Online Safety Act this week, a move Techdirt analyzes as a three-part strategic maneuver: imposing compliance costs that price out smaller AI competitors, redirecting legislative attention from AI-specific bills to social media regulation, and generating political cover for reputational damage from lawsuits alleging ChatGPT companion products contributed to youth suicides.

KOSA would require online platforms to adopt safer default settings, expanded parental controls, and a federal duty-of-care standard backed by FTC enforcement for minors. Lehane framed OpenAI's support as a complement to AI-specific safeguards, citing social media's past failures as a cautionary tale. Critics — the EFF, ACLU, and Techdirt — have argued consistently that KOSA's duty-of-care standard and parental control requirements would function as a content restriction and surveillance mandate because platforms facing undefined liability would over-restrict legal content for all users to reduce exposure, and because mandatory age-verification would require collecting government-ID-equivalent data from hundreds of millions of users. Techdirt identifies three strategic motivations: first, that KOSA compliance infrastructure is manageable for a capitalized incumbent but would be devastating for early-stage AI competitors; second, that backing social media regulation diverts Congressional attention from AI-specific bills that would directly constrain OpenAI's products; and third, that OpenAI faces litigation and reputational exposure from families alleging ChatGPT-based companion products contributed to teen suicides, and endorsing child safety legislation provides political protection.

Why it matters: KOSA has now passed the Senate once and is being reintroduced with growing corporate support; OpenAI's endorsement gives it significant new institutional momentum and may bring other AI companies into a coalition that accelerates passage. The regulatory capture dynamic Techdirt identifies matters because when dominant incumbents endorse regulation, the resulting rules tend to be designed around their compliance infrastructure rather than the actual harm, entrenching incumbents while generating collateral costs for users and small competitors. For the AI sector specifically, the concern is that KOSA — designed around social media's architecture — applied to AI companion products would require real-world identity verification, generating a novel high-value surveillance dataset whose breach risk, misuse potential, and law-enforcement access implications OpenAI has not publicly analyzed. The populations most likely to be harmed are those the law's supporters invoke: LGBTQ+ teenagers using AI tools for private exploration, minors seeking mental health information outside parental oversight, and young people without government ID. The endorsement also raises the structural question of whether any major tech company's backing of child-safety legislation should be taken at face value given the structural incentives to weaponize child-protection framing for competitive advantage.

entry.title: [tech law] State age-verification bills requiring OS-level identity checks leave Linux distributions with an impossible compliance choice: build surveillance infrastructure they cannot afford or block US states from downloading
entry.summary: A wave of US state laws mandating operating-system-level age verification — advancing in Louisiana, Illinois, Texas, Utah, and New York, plus the federal Parents Decide Act — is creating an existential compliance challenge for Linux distributions, which lack the centralized user databases and corporate revenue to implement the identity-check systems the bills require.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

A wave of US state laws mandating operating-system-level age verification — advancing in Louisiana, Illinois, Texas, Utah, and New York, plus the federal Parents Decide Act — is creating an existential compliance challenge for Linux distributions, which lack the centralized user databases and corporate revenue to implement the identity-check systems the bills require.

Multiple US states passed or are advancing laws in early 2026 requiring OS providers to verify user ages at device setup, typically through financial records, government-issued ID, or app-store account linkage, and to share that data via API with third parties. Louisiana HB 570 takes effect in July 2026; Illinois HB 5511 passed the House; Texas, Utah, and New York have similar measures advancing. At the federal level, H.R. 8250 — the Parents Decide Act, introduced April 2026 by Representatives Gottheimer and Stefanik — mandates OS-level age verification at setup. Linux distributions, collectively maintained by volunteer communities with no centralized revenue, customer databases, or identity relationships with end users, cannot implement the required systems. MX Linux, Zorin OS, Debian, Parrot OS, and Garuda Linux all issued statements in April and May 2026 refusing to implement age checks on privacy and architectural grounds; some indicated they may exclude US state IP ranges rather than comply. Colorado's bill was amended to exempt open-source operating systems after System76 CEO Carl Richell worked with Colorado Senator Matt Ball, but no equivalent exemptions exist in other state or federal bills.

Why it matters: The Linux compliance challenge exposes a structural flaw in age-gating legislation that assumes all software is delivered through centralized app stores with identity-linked accounts — the compliance architecture presupposes a corporate intermediary that simply does not exist in open-source software, where users download directly from project mirrors with no identity relationship with maintainers. If the federal Parents Decide Act passes without an open-source exemption, it would require Linux distributions to build identity verification infrastructure they lack the resources to construct and that would be architecturally incompatible with decentralized release processes. The practical outcome — Linux distributions blocking US state or national IP ranges — would reduce access to free, privacy-preserving computing for the users most likely to seek it: journalists, activists, abuse survivors, security researchers, and students. The legislative dynamic also reflects a broader pattern in which child-safety bills drafted around major commercial ecosystems (iOS and Android) create unexamined collateral damage to open-source infrastructure that underlies large portions of the internet's server and developer tooling, with potential downstream implications for server Linux distributions, developer tools, and embedded systems far beyond the end-user desktop that legislators have in mind.

entry.title: [tech law] Congress narrows GUARD Act to AI companion apps only, but amended bill retains mandatory real-world identity verification and raises per-violation penalties to $250,000, raising EFF concerns about chilling effects and market consolidation
entry.summary: An amended GUARD Act released in May 2026 narrows the AI age-restriction bill from covering all AI chatbots to targeting only AI companion applications presenting a persistent persona or simulating emotional relationships, but retains mandatory real-world identity verification for age checks and increases per-violation penalties from $100,000 to $250,000, enforceable by both federal and state officials.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

An amended GUARD Act released in May 2026 narrows the AI age-restriction bill from covering all AI chatbots to targeting only AI companion applications presenting a persistent persona or simulating emotional relationships, but retains mandatory real-world identity verification for age checks and increases per-violation penalties from $100,000 to $250,000, enforceable by both federal and state officials.

The original GUARD Act was criticized for sweeping in nearly every AI-powered conversational tool, including search engines, customer service bots, and general-purpose assistants like ChatGPT and Claude. The amended version limits scope to AI systems presenting a "persistent identity, persona or character" or engaging in "interactions involving emotional disclosures" — attempting to target apps like Replika or Character.AI. Despite the narrowed scope, the bill retains a "reasonable age verification" requirement tied to real-world identity data — financial records, government-issued ID, or app-store accounts — rather than self-certification or lower-friction alternatives. The per-violation fine rose from $100,000 to $250,000 and is now jointly enforceable by the FTC and state attorneys general. Critics note that the "emotional disclosure" and "persistent persona" definitions are broad enough to cover customer service chatbots that express sympathy, remember user preferences, or adapt tone over time, meaning the bill's actual scope remains substantially wider than its stated focus on companion AI. The EFF published analysis arguing that steep penalties combined with vague definitions will push developers — especially small ones — to block all underage users entirely rather than navigate uncertain legal standards.

Why it matters: The GUARD Act's trajectory illustrates a recurring dynamic in AI regulation: bills start broad, narrow their stated scope under pressure, but preserve the most consequential enforcement mechanisms — identity verification mandates and steep per-violation penalties — that drive compliance behavior regardless of definitional scope. The $250,000 per-violation structure matters because it is calibrated to be manageable for capitalized incumbents with legal and compliance teams but existential for early-stage AI startups; the predictable effect is de facto market consolidation favoring the largest players without any explicit market-structure intent. The mandatory real-world identity verification requirement is the bill's most consequential provision: AI companion developers would need to collect, store, and protect government-ID-equivalent data on their user base, creating a novel high-value surveillance dataset subject to breach risk, subpoena, and misuse potential. The vague "emotional disclosure" trigger guarantees litigation over which AI systems qualify, meaning the bill's actual scope will be defined through years of enforcement actions and court decisions rather than legislative text — a particularly poor outcome for small developers trying to assess compliance risk before investing in product development.

entry.title: [global politics] Trump-Xi Beijing summit ends: Xi walks Trump through Communist Party's inner compound, China lifts rare-earths freeze, Hormuz transit agreed, no Taiwan language in joint statement
entry.summary: The two-day Trump-Xi summit in Beijing concluded May 15 with Xi personally guiding Trump through Zhongnanhai — the Communist Party's centuries-old inner operational compound, entered by only a handful of foreign heads of state — while delivering his clearest direct Taiwan warning yet and reaching substantive outcomes on rare earths, Boeing jets, Hormuz transit, and a three-year strategic stability framework, but producing no joint statement language on Taiwan.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The two-day Trump-Xi summit in Beijing concluded May 15 with Xi personally guiding Trump through Zhongnanhai — the Communist Party's centuries-old inner operational compound, entered by only a handful of foreign heads of state — while delivering his clearest direct Taiwan warning yet and reaching substantive outcomes on rare earths, Boeing jets, Hormuz transit, and a three-year strategic stability framework, but producing no joint statement language on Taiwan.

Trump arrived in Beijing May 13 for the first US presidential state visit to China in nearly a decade, accompanied by Apple CEO Tim Cook, Tesla CEO Elon Musk, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The summit covered trade and tariffs, Taiwan, the Iran war, and AI governance guardrails. On trade, China agreed to order 200 Boeing jets and to lift the rare-earths export restrictions imposed in 2026 as leverage in tariff negotiations — restrictions affecting semiconductor fabrication timelines, electric vehicle battery supply chains, and US defense procurement for systems relying on neodymium and dysprosium. On the Iran war, both leaders agreed the Strait of Hormuz — through which roughly 20% of global LNG flows — must remain open to commercial shipping, marking the first time China formally weighed in on the conflict's key chokepoint. Xi and Trump agreed on "strategic stability" as a framework for bilateral relations for the next three years. Xi issued his clearest direct Taiwan warning to Trump: mishandling the issue would put the relationship in "great jeopardy" with "clashes and even conflicts" a real possibility. The joint statement contains no Taiwan language, reflecting the two sides' deliberate avoidance of formal commitment on the most sensitive issue.

Why it matters: Xi's direct verbal Taiwan warning is the summit's most significant diplomatic output — not because it changes China's stated position, which has been consistent for decades, but because it was delivered in person to a president with a track record of unpredictability on Taiwan and who tends to respond to direct interpersonal appeals. The Zhongnanhai visit carries deliberate symbolic weight: access to the compound is calibrated to convey the highest tier of diplomatic respect and is extended to very few foreign leaders, signaling that Xi views the relationship as requiring a unique setting to communicate seriousness. The lifting of the rare-earths freeze has immediate industrial and defense significance, since prolonged restrictions would have forced costly supply chain diversification for US and European semiconductor, EV, and defense manufacturers. The absence of Taiwan in the joint statement means the two sides papered over their deepest structural disagreement, leaving the same risk intact despite the warm atmospherics of a rose-garden stroll. The presence of Musk, Cook, and Huang in the delegation raises ongoing questions about corporate influence in diplomatic settings, particularly given Musk's dual role as Trump advisor and Tesla CEO with critical Shanghai manufacturing exposure.

entry.title: [global politics] Russia kills 24 including three children in Kyiv apartment strike — deadliest attack on the capital since the invasion — as part of war's largest-ever barrage: 1,560 drones in two days immediately after US-brokered ceasefire expired
entry.summary: A Russian cruise missile struck a nine-story Kyiv apartment building on May 14-15, killing at least 24 people including three children and destroying all 18 apartments in the affected corner — the deadliest single attack on the Ukrainian capital since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion — as part of Russia's largest-ever aerial assault: more than 1,560 drones and dozens of missiles in two days, launched immediately after a brief US-brokered May 9-11 ceasefire expired.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

A Russian cruise missile struck a nine-story Kyiv apartment building on May 14-15, killing at least 24 people including three children and destroying all 18 apartments in the affected corner — the deadliest single attack on the Ukrainian capital since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion — as part of Russia's largest-ever aerial assault: more than 1,560 drones and dozens of missiles in two days, launched immediately after a brief US-brokered May 9-11 ceasefire expired.

The Russian assault resumed immediately after the May 9-11 ceasefire window that US President Trump said he had asked both Zelenskyy and Putin to observe. Russia launched more than 1,560 drones between Wednesday and Thursday, along with dozens of ballistic missiles — the largest aerial offensive in the war by drone count. Ukrainian air defenses shot down or jammed 693 aerial targets in a single overnight period, including 41 missiles and 652 drones, but multiple warheads penetrated Kyiv's defensive perimeter. The cruise missile that struck the nine-story apartment building destroyed all 18 apartments in the affected corner and killed 24 confirmed dead, including three children; Zelenskyy reported 48 wounded in Kyiv alone, including two more children. In total, 180 sites across Ukraine were damaged in the barrage, including more than 50 residential buildings. The UN senior humanitarian coordinator issued a public statement calling the attacks a clear violation of international humanitarian law. Ukraine retaliated by striking a Russian industrial facility with long-range missiles.

Why it matters: The timing of Russia's largest-ever aerial barrage — launched immediately after a Trump-brokered ceasefire and during Trump's state visit to Beijing — signals that Moscow is not treating Trump's mediation as a meaningful operational constraint, which directly undercuts the US argument that Trump's personal diplomacy is reducing the war's intensity. Russia's decision to escalate to its highest-ever single-campaign drone count in the ceasefire's immediate aftermath appears designed to demonstrate that ceasefire windows are tactical pauses rather than strategic turning points — a message directed simultaneously at Ukraine, the Trump administration, and NATO allies. The ICC, which holds an existing arrest warrant for Putin, will be documenting civilian targeting patterns from this barrage for future prosecutorial proceedings, and the incident will be referenced in ongoing discussions about applying the Rome Statute's provisions on deliberate targeting of civilian infrastructure. For NATO and US military planners, the barrage and Ukraine's interception of 693 of 1,600-plus incoming targets provides critical operational data on air defense saturation thresholds and the resourcing levels needed to maintain meaningful coverage — data that will directly inform discussions about expanding PATRIOT and HIMARS interceptor supplies.

entry.title: [ai] Musk v. Altman closing arguments complete — Musk lawyers accuse Altman of 'selective amnesia' and self-dealing; OpenAI argues lawsuit is time-barred; advisory jury deliberates next week in landmark AI governance trial
entry.summary: Closing arguments concluded May 14 in Musk v. OpenAI, the landmark federal trial in Oakland over whether OpenAI and Sam Altman betrayed the organization's nonprofit mission for personal gain, with Musk's lawyer accusing Altman of 'selective amnesia' and systematic self-dealing while OpenAI's counsel countered that the lawsuit was filed too late and Musk's own conduct bars recovery; the advisory jury is expected to return a verdict next week.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Closing arguments concluded May 14 in Musk v. OpenAI, the landmark federal trial in Oakland over whether OpenAI and Sam Altman betrayed the organization's nonprofit mission for personal gain, with Musk's lawyer accusing Altman of 'selective amnesia' and systematic self-dealing while OpenAI's counsel countered that the lawsuit was filed too late and Musk's own conduct bars recovery; the advisory jury is expected to return a verdict next week.

Elon Musk filed the lawsuit in 2023 alleging that OpenAI and its executives — primarily Sam Altman and Greg Brockman — violated the organization's founding nonprofit mission by converting to a for-profit structure and enriching themselves through stock grants and transactions with entities in which they held financial interests. Trial began in late April 2026 in federal court in Oakland before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, with testimony from Musk, Altman, former chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, former COO Mira Murati, and former board members Helen Toner and Tasha McCauley. In closing argument, Musk's lawyer Steven Molo argued Altman's credibility was undercut by former colleagues' testimony and characterized Altman's accounts of key early governance commitments as "selective amnesia." OpenAI's lawyers Sarah Eddy and William Savitt countered that Altman and Brockman made no binding commitments to Musk about corporate structure, that Musk's donations were properly spent, that the lawsuit was barred by the statute of limitations, and that Musk's own conduct should equitably preclude his recovery. Because the jury's role is advisory in this bench trial, Judge Gonzalez Rogers makes the final liability determination; a remedies phase begins Monday.

The testimony from Sutskever and Murati — both of whom departed OpenAI under circumstances involving disagreements with Altman's leadership — will be closely evaluated by Judge Gonzalez Rogers for credibility, since their accounts directly contradict Altman's version of key governance decisions. The feature integrates with Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger, and native iOS and Android messaging apps, as well as third-party apps with standard text input interfaces. Meta simultaneously enabled the teleprompter feature broadly — projecting text into the glasses' field of view for the wearer to read — after its CES preview. The neural handwriting feature is the most significant new capability for the Ray-Ban Display since launch.

Why it matters: The commercial deployment of EMG-based text input at scale is a milestone in human-computer interaction because it is the first time a mainstream consumer product has used muscle signals — rather than touch, voice, or gaze — as the primary text input modality for messaging, and the broad rollout will generate real-world accuracy and user adoption data that will directly inform the next generation of neural interface design across the industry. For Apple, which has signaled interest in neural interfaces through acquisitions including EMG startup Proxima in 2024 and whose AR glasses roadmap is expected to include similar capabilities, Meta's execution at consumer scale demonstrates that EMG input is viable outside research or clinical settings, compressing Apple's response timeline. entry.title: [tech law] Federal judge permanently bars DOGE from reinstating ChatGPT-driven cuts to $100M in NEH humanities grants, ruling the process unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination
entry.summary: US District Judge Colleen McMahon on May 8 permanently barred the Trump administration from reinstating DOGE's termination of roughly 1,400 National Endowment for the Humanities grants, ruling in a 143-page opinion that DOGE staffers' use of ChatGPT and DEI keyword lists to identify grants for elimination constituted unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination under the First and Fifth Amendments.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

US District Judge Colleen McMahon on May 8 permanently barred the Trump administration from reinstating DOGE's termination of roughly 1,400 National Endowment for the Humanities grants, ruling in a 143-page opinion that DOGE staffers' use of ChatGPT and DEI keyword lists to identify grants for elimination constituted unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination under the First and Fifth Amendments.

Between April 1 and April 3, 2025, two DOGE staffers — Justin Fox and Nate Cavanaugh — eliminated roughly 1,400 NEH grants collectively worth more than $100 million. Depositions revealed that Fox copied and pasted ChatGPT-generated "DEI rationales" into spreadsheets, using keyword searches for terms including "DEI," "Equity," "Inclusion," "BIPOC," and "LGBTQ" to flag grants for termination. Projects cut included an anthology of short fiction by Jewish writers from the Soviet Union about Holocaust survival, Native American oral history archives, African American history projects, and women's studies grants. Judge McMahon found that the NEH grants officer who formally approved the terminations lacked the legal authority to cancel them, and that even if she had, the mechanism was unconstitutionally discriminatory because government funding cannot be conditioned on viewpoint. McMahon devoted an entire section of her opinion to rejecting the administration's "ChatGPT defense," invoking comedian Flip Wilson's "the Devil made me do it" line to note that the AI chatbot's role did not insulate the government from constitutional accountability. The ruling was not accompanied by a stay, meaning the grant terminations remain permanently blocked pending any appeal.

Why it matters: The ruling is the most detailed judicial accounting yet of how AI tools can be used by government actors in discriminatory ways, and McMahon's logic — that deploying an AI chatbot to execute a discriminatory purpose does not make the discrimination any less constitutional — will become a critical precedent for future challenges to AI-assisted government decision-making across any agency that uses automated systems to allocate, terminate, or restrict government benefits. The First Amendment viewpoint discrimination finding is particularly potent: it means any future administration that uses content-based keywords to cut funding to disfavored academic or cultural work will face the same constitutional bar, regardless of what technology is used to identify targets. The ruling also signals that courts will scrutinize not just the formal decision-maker but the actual operative process, since DOGE staffers acted far outside their delegated authority. If the administration appeals to the Second Circuit, it faces an unfavorable record given how explicitly McMahon documented the discriminatory mechanics from deposition testimony, making the path to reversal narrow.

Trump arrived in Beijing on May 13 for his first visit to China as president since 2017 — the first time a sitting US president has visited China in nearly a decade — accompanied by a delegation including Apple CEO Tim Cook, Tesla CEO Elon Musk, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, signaling the visit's economic dimension. The joint statement, notably, contains no mention of Taiwan — China's insistence on outcome language that avoids the word entirely. On the Iran war, both leaders agreed the Strait of Hormuz must remain open to commercial shipping; Xi's involvement marks the first time China has formally weighed in on the conflict's key chokepoint.

Why it matters: Xi's Taiwan warning is the most consequential public statement to emerge from any US-China summit in years: it was delivered directly to Trump in Beijing, not through a communiqué or diplomatic channel, which means Trump cannot later claim ignorance of the red line China considers existential. The lifting of the rare-earths freeze has immediate industrial significance — the export restrictions had begun affecting semiconductor fabrication timelines, battery supply chains, and US defense procurement for systems including F-35 components and guided munitions that rely on neodymium and dysprosium. The Hormuz agreement is significant for the Iran war: it implicitly acknowledges China's role as a mediator or at least a floor-setter for conflict boundaries, giving Beijing a formal stake in keeping its own oil supply lines intact. The notable absence of Taiwan in the joint statement means the two sides likely papered over their deepest disagreement, leaving the same structural tension intact. Why it matters: Latvia's government collapse over this incident reveals a structural tension that every NATO ally bordering Ukraine or Russia must manage: how to publicly support Ukrainian military operations while also holding Ukraine accountable for errant strikes or airspace violations on allied territory. The political implications go beyond Latvia — similar drone overflights have occurred in Romania and other NATO states, and each time the host government must choose between absorbing domestic political costs or confronting Ukraine diplomatically. The October 2026 election timing means Latvia will be governed by a caretaker administration during one of the most critical periods of the war, potentially affecting its foreign policy coordination. Nigeria's Federal High Court on May 13 sentenced former Minister of Power Saleh Mamman to a cumulative 75-year prison term in absentia after convicting him on all 12 counts of money laundering and indirect conversion of ₦33.8 billion in public funds earmarked for the Mambilla and Zungeru hydroelectric projects during the Buhari administration.

Justice James Omotosho of the Federal High Court in Abuja, acting on prosecution brought by Nigeria's Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), convicted Mamman — who served as Minister of Power between 2019 and 2021 under former President Muhammadu Buhari — on all 12 counts related to the diversion of funds allocated to two major national infrastructure projects: the Mambilla hydroelectric project (a long-delayed 3,050 MW dam on the Taraba River, one of Africa's most ambitious power projects) and the Zungeru hydroelectric dam (700 MW, located in Niger State). Justice Omotosho ordered the sentences on each of the 12 counts to run consecutively rather than concurrently, transforming individual terms of approximately six years per count into a cumulative 75-year sentence. Mamman was not present in court for sentencing, and his current whereabouts were not confirmed at the time of judgment. He becomes the first minister who served under former President Buhari to be jailed for corruption, a notable milestone given the scale of corruption allegations that surrounded the 2015–2023 Buhari era despite the administration's anti-corruption rhetoric.

Why it matters: The conviction is genuinely rare for Nigeria's anti-corruption framework: previous high-profile cases against senior Buhari-era officials either stalled, ended in acquittals, or resulted in plea bargains with minimal custodial sentences. The consecutive sentencing — an unusual judicial choice — appears designed to signal that the court viewed the 12-count scheme as an aggravated pattern of conduct warranting punishment beyond what concurrent sentences would convey, and to maximize deterrence for ministerial-level corruption. The Mambilla project specifically has been plagued by contractor disputes and funding scandals for decades; the conviction adds legal accountability to what has been an emblematic failure of Nigerian infrastructure planning. The in absentia nature of the verdict introduces immediate enforcement complexity: Mamman must be located and extradited or surrendered before the sentence can be served, and Nigeria's record of executing foreign extradition requests is mixed. The EFCC's success in this case may signal a more aggressive posture under the current Tinubu administration toward prosecuting predecessors' officials, though critics will note that the political incentive to pursue Buhari-era figures is different from the political incentive to pursue allies of the current government.

The attack began just before 1 a.m. Kyiv time when a nationwide aerial alert warned that Russia had launched MiG-31 bombers capable of carrying ballistic-missile payloads, placing every region of Ukraine simultaneously at risk. The 675 drones and 56 missiles fired represent one of the most massive single-night strikes of the entire invasion. The attack comes just three days after the 72-hour Victory Day ceasefire brokered by President Trump (May 9-11) collapsed almost immediately upon announcement, with Russia launching more than 200 Shahed-type drones the very night the ceasefire formally expired. Ukraine's air defenses intercepted the majority of incoming drones and missiles, but with 675 projectiles in the air simultaneously, achieving 100% intercept is practically impossible.

The fact that the attack came three days after the expiration of Trump's Victory Day ceasefire signals that Moscow views the ceasefire framework as an opportunity to reposition rather than a genuine de-escalation commitment — a pattern that significantly constrains US diplomatic leverage in future negotiations, since Russia has now established a clear precedent of resuming at higher intensity when pauses end. Cuba's energy collapse has been building since December 2025, when the United States seized tankers carrying Venezuelan oil destined for Cuba as part of the escalating US-Venezuela confrontation. A Trump executive order signed in January 2026 threatened tariffs on any country shipping fuel to Cuba, effectively halting exports from Mexico and Venezuela — previously Cuba's two top suppliers — and deterring tankers from any other nation. Only one shipload of donated Russian oil reached Cuba after the blockade took effect; by early May 2026, that supply was exhausted. Minister de la O announced on state-run media on May 14: "We have absolutely no fuel oil, and absolutely no diesel," adding that the national grid is in a "critical" state. In Havana, residents are experiencing blackouts of up to 22 hours per day, triggering protests across multiple neighborhoods by people who describe the situation as no longer tolerable. Cuba has a population of nearly 10 million, and the energy system underpins not just residential power but hospitals, water pumping stations, food refrigeration, and public transportation — making a system-wide collapse far more severe than a managed rolling blackout.

Why it matters: This is a humanitarian emergency with cascading effects: 22-hour daily blackouts in a tropical climate in May mean failing medical equipment in hospitals, no refrigeration for food and medicine, compromised water supply in buildings relying on electric pumps, and severe disruption to every sector of the Cuban economy. Cuba has managed prolonged US sanctions since 1962, but a system-wide fuel collapse without any near-term resupply prospect is qualitatively different from prior energy crises. The political question is whether the US blockade accelerates regime collapse or produces the kind of civilian hardship that enables repression rather than reform — historical precedent from Cuba suggests the government typically tightens control during crises rather than liberalizing. For the Trump-Xi summit now underway in Beijing, Cuba is a secondary but real pressure point: China has been pressing Trump on his Latin America policy, and visible humanitarian suffering in a 10-million-person island nation creates diplomatic leverage for critics at the UN and OAS. Trump's tariff threat against third-country shippers of fuel to Cuba will also likely face a WTO challenge, and whether any non-US ally is willing to test that threat by sending fuel shipments will be an early indicator of how far US economic coercion can extend against third parties under the current trade law framework.

entry.title: [ai] South Africa's national AI policy was written by AI and cited four non-existent sources; government withdraws it within days
entry.summary: South Africa's first national AI policy — released in April 2026 and intended to govern AI-generated misinformation risks — was withdrawn after researcher Damien Charlotin discovered at least four citations were AI hallucinations that do not correspond to any real publication, prompting the Minister of Communications to acknowledge the government had failed its own standard of human oversight of AI outputs.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

South Africa's first national AI policy — released in April 2026 and intended to govern AI-generated misinformation risks — was withdrawn after researcher Damien Charlotin discovered at least four citations were AI hallucinations that do not correspond to any real publication, prompting the Minister of Communications to acknowledge the government had failed its own standard of human oversight of AI outputs.

South Africa's Department of Communications and Digital Technologies circulated a draft national AI policy in April 2026 — the country's first such framework — that addressed the risks posed by AI-generated misinformation and proposed governance structures for responsible AI deployment. Damien Charlotin, a researcher who had built specialized software to detect hallucinated citations in AI-generated text, ran the policy document through his verification platform and identified at least four citations that do not correspond to any real academic paper, regulatory document, or publication. The citations appear to have been hallucinated by the AI language model used to draft portions of the policy, and were included in the official government document without verification. Charlotin flagged the findings publicly via LinkedIn and his platform, prompting immediate media coverage and government attention. Minister of Communications Solly Malatsi publicly acknowledged the failure within days, stating: "The most plausible explanation is that AI-generated citations were included without proper verification. This should not have happened." He characterized the incident as compromising "the integrity and credibility of the draft policy" and framed it as precisely the kind of problem the policy itself was meant to prevent. The government withdrew the full policy proposal within days, committing to a rewrite with proper verification procedures.

Why it matters: The governance paradox is sharp: a document designed to regulate AI hallucination was itself compromised by AI hallucination before a single regulation took effect. The South Africa case joins a documented pattern of institutional AI drafting failures — including the 2023 Mata v. Avianca case where a US attorney submitted ChatGPT-generated briefs with fabricated case citations, and multiple government reports with non-existent sources — that reflects a systemic underestimation of how confidently AI language models confabulate plausible-sounding but false references. For national AI policy globally, the incident underscores that citation verification must be a mandatory and human-executed step in any AI-assisted government drafting, and that this check cannot itself be delegated to another AI tool. More troubling for South Africa specifically is what the incident reveals about the institutional review process: Charlotin's specialized software found the hallucinations that the Ministry's own review procedure missed, raising questions about what quality assurance steps were actually in place for the country's first national AI framework. The withdrawal and rewrite will delay South Africa's AI regulatory capacity by months, leaving the country without national guidance during a critical window when AI is being rapidly deployed in both government and private sector contexts across the continent.

Israeli drone and missile strikes across Lebanon on May 13 killed at least 12 people including two children, with eight of the dead struck on vehicles traveling the coastal highway linking Beirut to the south — attacks that occurred on the eve of scheduled US-mediated peace talks and raise serious questions under international humanitarian law about targeting of civilian transport routes.

May 13's strikes were part of the ongoing 2026 Lebanon war, a renewed conflict that resumed in early 2026 following the expiration of the November 2024 Hezbollah ceasefire. The day's attacks were concentrated on the coastal road linking Beirut to southern Lebanon — a primary civilian supply and transit route — with eight people killed in three separate drone strikes on vehicles. Additional strikes killed three people in the Tyre district and one near Sidon. Among the dead were two children and two Lebanese Civil Defence paramedics. Sources cited by multiple outlets put the overall May 13 toll between 12 and 15, with discrepancies reflecting different Lebanese health ministry and media counts from the same day's events. Earlier in May, Israel had struck Beirut proper for the first time since a ceasefire framework had been nominally in effect, reportedly targeting a Hezbollah commander. The May 13 attacks came one day before scheduled US-mediated talks intended to establish a new ceasefire framework, prompting Lebanese officials and international observers to argue the strikes were designed to degrade Hezbollah mobility ahead of negotiations while demonstrating Israel's continued operational tempo.

Why it matters: Strikes concentrated on civilian vehicles on a major civilian highway — rather than military installations — are legally significant under international humanitarian law: the principle of distinction requires parties to distinguish between civilian and military targets, and IHL's proportionality rule requires that civilian harm not be excessive relative to the anticipated military advantage. Human rights organizations including Amnesty International are documenting individual strikes for potential ICC proceedings, and the killing of two children and two paramedics is likely to feature prominently in any future accountability process. The eve-of-talks timing signals that neither Israel nor Hezbollah has committed to a genuine ceasefire framework, and conducting lethal strikes during the day before US-mediated negotiations creates pressure on the US mediators to either accept continued military operations as a fait accompli or risk a diplomatic walkout by Lebanese parties. Lebanon's civilian infrastructure continues to erode with each escalation, and aid organizations warn that Beirut's ability to function as a commercial and governance center is at serious risk if the conflict continues through the summer tourism season that historically drives a significant portion of the Lebanese economy.

entry.title: [law] DOJ attorney admits DHS press release attacking federal judge was false; judge weighs contempt for DHS and DOJ
entry.summary: A Rhode Island federal judge is weighing contempt proceedings against DHS and the DOJ after Assistant US Attorney Kevin Bolan admitted in open court that a DHS press release headlined "Activist Biden Judge Releases Violent Criminal Illegal Alien Wanted for Murder" was "simply not true" — because he had withheld the key fact from the judge at ICE's instruction while DHS used it to publicly attack her.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

A Rhode Island federal judge is weighing contempt proceedings against DHS and the DOJ after Assistant US Attorney Kevin Bolan admitted in open court that a DHS press release headlined "Activist Biden Judge Releases Violent Criminal Illegal Alien Wanted for Murder" was "simply not true" — because he had withheld the key fact from the judge at ICE's instruction while DHS used it to publicly attack her.

The case centers on ICE detainee Bryan Rafael Gomez, a Dominican national whom US District Judge Melissa DuBose of the District of Rhode Island ordered released on bail after a bail hearing. Following that release, DHS published a press release attacking Judge DuBose as an "activist Biden judge" who had "released a violent criminal illegal alien wanted for murder" — implying she knew about a Dominican Republic murder warrant against Gomez and released him anyway. In open court on May 13, AUSA Kevin Bolan admitted the press release was false: ICE had instructed him not to disclose the Dominican murder warrant to Judge DuBose at the bail hearing, meaning she lacked the information when making her ruling — the very information DHS was then using to portray her as reckless. The contradiction was compounded by the fact that DHS itself had disclosed the warrant in a separate press release on April 16, making ICE's instruction to withhold it from the court particularly indefensible. Bolan filed a written admission — "The press release simply was not true" — and apologized to the court. Judge DuBose stated the false press release had "put her security at risk" by publicly mischaracterizing her judicial conduct. She is now considering contempt proceedings primarily against DHS, whose press release remains posted, with potential separate findings for the DOJ over Bolan's failure to disclose material information to the court.

Why it matters: A contempt finding against a federal agency for the content of a public press release would be historically significant — agencies are rarely held in contempt for external communications — but the DOJ's own written admission that the press release was false eliminates the government's most obvious defense. The structural conduct is particularly serious: ICE instructed its lawyer to withhold information from the court, then used that withheld information to create a press release implying the judge acted recklessly on information she never received. This is not a matter of spin or contested characterization; it is a case where the government's own attorney admitted the agency's public claim was false. Chief Justice Roberts warned explicitly in both 2025 and 2026 that attacks on the independence and integrity of the judiciary by the executive branch undermine the constitutional order; this case is an instance of exactly that conduct — and unlike abstract rhetoric, it created a documented, specific safety risk to a named federal judge. If Judge DuBose issues a contempt order, it will establish that federal agencies cannot misrepresent judicial proceedings in public communications without consequence, and will likely trigger appeals that reach the circuit court and potentially the Supreme Court on the scope of judicial authority to sanction executive agency speech.

entry.summary: German and US law enforcement arrested Owe Martin Andresen, 49, in a May 7 raid in Germany, charging him as the main administrator of Dream Market — which at its peak hosted over 100,000 listings and facilitated trafficking of 90 kg of heroin, 450 kg of cocaine, and 36 kg of fentanyl — as he faces a maximum of 240 years in US federal prison and up to five years in Germany.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

German and US law enforcement arrested Owe Martin Andresen, 49, in a May 7 raid in Germany, charging him as the main administrator of Dream Market — which at its peak hosted over 100,000 listings and facilitated trafficking of 90 kg of heroin, 450 kg of cocaine, and 36 kg of fentanyl — as he faces a maximum of 240 years in US federal prison and up to five years in Germany.

Dream Market launched in 2013 as a Tor-based, cryptocurrency-accepting dark web marketplace and became the dominant second-generation successor platform to Silk Road after the FBI seized that site in October 2013. At its peak, Dream Market hosted over 100,000 listings for illegal goods including narcotics, stolen personal data, and counterfeit documents. The DOJ's unsealed indictment charges that the platform facilitated trafficking of 90 kilograms of heroin, 450 kilograms of cocaine, 25 kilograms of crack cocaine, and 36 kilograms of fentanyl, among other contraband. Andresen, a Norwegian national, is charged with six counts of money laundering and six counts of international money laundering, with DOJ alleging he laundered approximately $2 million between August 2023 and April 2025. The arrest followed a joint raid by German and US investigators on three locations in Germany on May 7, 2026. US Attorney Theodore Hertzberg confirmed that Andresen "will be prosecuted in both Germany and the United States." Dream Market itself closed in April 2019, making the investigation a years-long effort to identify and locate its anonymous administrator.

Why it matters: The arrest demonstrates that DOJ and European law enforcement pursue dark web marketplace operators for years after their platforms close — a powerful deterrent message to current platform administrators who believe shutting down before law enforcement acts will shield them from prosecution. Dream Market was among the platforms that professionalized the dark web drug trade by introducing user reviews, escrow systems, dispute resolution, and vendor ratings that made purchases more reliable and thereby drove adoption; the accountability of its administrator matters not just symbolically but because it closes an accountability gap that has persisted since the platform's 2019 closure. The money laundering charges are particularly significant because they establish the principle that platform administrators are criminally liable for the proceeds flowing through their systems even when they never physically touched any drugs — a theory that prosecutors have progressively strengthened by improving their ability to trace and charge cryptocurrency flows, making the "cryptocurrency anonymity" defense increasingly ineffective. This case follows the 2024 sentencing of AlphaBay founder DeSnake and the 2025 conviction of Hydra Market administrators, confirming a pattern of DOJ eventually closing cases on every major dark web platform from the 2013-2020 era regardless of the time elapsed.

entry.title: [tech law] Trump administration defends in court its right to expel disinformation researchers and content moderation experts from the US on First Amendment grounds
entry.summary: At a May 13 hearing in Washington DC, the Trump administration told Judge Boasberg it has the right to deny visas and deport foreign nationals who work in disinformation research and content moderation, as the Coalition for Independent Technology Research argued the Rubio visa policy violates the First Amendment rights of its US citizen members to associate with and hear from foreign colleagues.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

At a May 13 hearing in Washington DC, the Trump administration told Judge Boasberg it has the right to deny visas and deport foreign nationals who work in disinformation research and content moderation, as the Coalition for Independent Technology Research argued the Rubio visa policy violates the First Amendment rights of its US citizen members to associate with and hear from foreign colleagues.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a policy in May 2025 authorizing the State Department to deny visas to foreign nationals whose work is deemed to "facilitate censorship of Americans," which the government interprets to include content moderation, disinformation and misinformation research, fact-checking, and trust and safety work. In December 2025, consular officers were instructed to scrutinize applicants for evidence of such activities. The policy has already been applied to ban five European nationals including former EU Tech Commissioner Thierry Breton — who had public confrontations with Elon Musk over X's DSA compliance — and Imran Ahmed, CEO of the Center for Countering Digital Hate, whose deportation was temporarily blocked by a federal judge. The Coalition for Independent Technology Research — an organization of US academics and analysts — sued in March 2026 on First Amendment grounds, represented by the Knight First Amendment Institute and Protect Democracy, arguing that the policy chills the rights of CITR's US citizen members to receive communications from and collaborate with foreign scholars in their fields. At the May 13 hearing, Judge James Boasberg described the case as "quite complex" and identified four areas requiring further briefing before he could act: whether one or multiple policies are at issue; whether CITR and/or individual members have standing; the First Amendment merits; and available legal remedies if the policy is struck down.

Why it matters: The case presents a direct constitutional challenge to a structural feature of the Trump administration's approach to online speech: using immigration law as a mechanism for suppressing viewpoints the executive branch dislikes, framed counterintuitively as a First Amendment defense. The administration's claim that content moderation expertise "facilitates censorship" inverts the conventional understanding — the scholars being targeted study how platforms enforce their rules, and characterizing that study as censorship requires accepting a theory of free speech under which platforms have no constitutional authority to moderate at all, a position the Supreme Court specifically declined to adopt in Moody v. NetChoice (2024). If the Rubio visa policy survives First Amendment challenge, it will establish that the government can effectively exile entire academic disciplines from the United States by categorizing their work as speech restriction, which would have severe consequences for the US's ability to attract and retain global academic talent in social media safety research at exactly the moment when AI-generated disinformation is accelerating in scale and sophistication. Judge Boasberg's reluctance to act quickly signals the case will proceed through full merits briefing, meaning the policy could remain in effect for a year or more while the litigation progresses — a significant win for the administration regardless of ultimate outcome.

entry.title: [tech law] EU Commission president calls for minimum age law for social media as Digital Fairness Act takes shape
entry.summary: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen declared that discussions about minimum-age requirements for social media “can no longer be ignored,” signaling that a legislative proposal could emerge by summer 2026 as part of the Digital Fairness Act, which will go beyond the DSA to target addictive design features.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen declared that discussions about minimum-age requirements for social media “can no longer be ignored,” signaling that a legislative proposal could emerge by summer 2026 as part of the Digital Fairness Act, which will go beyond the DSA to target addictive design features.

Von der Leyen announced that an expert panel would deliver recommendations within weeks and that a legal proposal could emerge by summer 2026, though the European Parliament must ultimately pass any legislation. The move reflects a significant acceleration of EU platform regulation: the Digital Services Act, which entered full force in February 2024, already requires platforms to protect minors from harmful content and conduct risk assessments, but it does not set a minimum age and relies on platforms’ own enforcement. The forthcoming Digital Fairness Act would target what regulators describe as “attention-capturing mechanisms, complex terms, and subscription traps” — design patterns the Commission believes are deliberately deployed to maximize engagement at the expense of user wellbeing. Multiple EU member states are already moving independently: Spain, Greece, Norway, France, Denmark, Turkey, and the Netherlands are all considering or implementing age verification protocols. Separately, the Commission is investigating Meta for potential DSA violations involving insufficient protections for minors on Instagram and Facebook, and a separate probe is examining xAI’s Grok nudification capabilities.

Why it matters: A Commission-level age restriction law would be the EU’s most aggressive intervention into social media platform design to date, going beyond content moderation to regulate the fundamental architecture of recommendation and engagement systems. The legal instrument will likely require age verification at the platform level — a technically and privacy-controversial mechanism, since effective age verification requires collecting identity data that itself creates privacy risks. Privacy experts including the IAPP’s Isabelle Roccia have noted that Commission-level action is important precisely to prevent fragmentation: if seven member states implement seven different age verification regimes, the resulting compliance burden for platforms could paradoxically harm the single market. For tech companies, the combination of the DSA’s existing obligations, the forthcoming DFA, and active investigations into Meta and xAI signals that the EU is moving from “platforms must assess risks” to “platforms must demonstrate specific design outcomes” — a regulatory posture that will require significant product changes, not just policy updates.

President Trump landed in Beijing on Wednesday for a two-day summit with President Xi Jinping — the first visit by a US leader to China since Trump’s own 2017 trip — with trade tariffs, Taiwan, the Iran war, and AI governance all on the agenda.

Trump arrived in Beijing accompanied by a delegation of senior business executives as well as Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. The summit, originally planned for March, was delayed following US and Israeli strikes on Iran. On trade, Trump’s aggressive use of tariffs was significantly curtailed in February when the Supreme Court struck down his global “reciprocal” tariffs as unconstitutional; a residual 10% baseline tariff is currently the subject of Federal Circuit proceedings. China is expected to press for full tariff rollback while Trump is seeking to avoid new domestic economic pain from his own trade policy. On Taiwan, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Secretary Rubio on April 30 that Taiwan is “the biggest point of risk” in the relationship, and Beijing is expected to seek concrete assurances that the US will not further strengthen arms sales or diplomatic recognition of Taipei. On Iran, Washington wants Beijing to use its leverage as the purchaser of more than 80% of Iranian crude oil exports to press Tehran toward a ceasefire deal; China’s position has been publicly neutral while benefiting economically from discounted Iranian oil.

Why it matters: This is arguably the most consequential bilateral summit in the world right now, touching three overlapping crises simultaneously: an active war involving Iran where China holds unique economic leverage, a Taiwan Strait tension that could escalate into military confrontation, and a trade war whose resolution would reshape global supply chains. Trump’s Supreme Court defeat on tariffs has shifted US bargaining leverage — Beijing knows any new tariff threats face constitutional hurdles — so the summit outcome will reveal how Trump’s trade strategy adapts to judicial constraints. On Iran, China’s willingness to pressure Tehran is the single variable most likely to determine whether a ceasefire holds or breaks down; a concrete commitment from Xi would be the summit’s most significant deliverable. AI governance may emerge as an unexpected area of bilateral agreement, since both governments have an interest in preventing AI-enabled military escalation between nuclear powers, even as they compete fiercely on AI capability.
